clips.start_words: What kind of capsule are they using
clips.send: Someone who just bought a year's supply of vitamins sends this to the friend who talked them into it: one line on the bottle they never read - the unease of finding out after you already paid for it.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau on the one word to find on your supplement bottle before you swallow anything.

Many vitamin and mineral capsules are plastic, the same material as a water bottle, just small enough to swallow. His advice: flip the bottle over and read the ingredient list. It should say cellulose capsule, ideally organic cellulose capsule.

If it doesn't say that, he says skip the whole bottle, not just that one ingredient.

Go check your own bottle right now. What does it say?

clips.send: A meal-prepper sends this to the friend who eats the same chicken and rice every day: the body doesn't want the same thing twice - the nagging doubt of wondering if your routine is working against you.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau's point about why your body resists routine.

You already do this without thinking: salad one day, spinach the next, chicken today, fish tomorrow, rice one night, potatoes the next. Nobody eats the exact same meal every single day, because the body isn't designed to live on repetition.

His argument: that's exactly why taking the identical supplement, in the identical amount, every day of the year, works against the same body that insists on variety at every meal.

When's the last time you ate the same thing two days running?

#kevintrudeau #nutrition #foodtruth #wbdaily #healthyeating #wholefood

clips.start_words: You'd have to eat five times
clips.send: A home cook sends this to the grandparent who always says food doesn't taste like it used to: the actual reason, backed by a doctor's math - the quiet grief of realizing today's food is thinner than it looks.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau cites a doctor's claim that you'd need to eat five times as much food today to get the nutrition your grandparents got from one plate, decades ago.

His proof is one you can test yourself. Cut an onion from decades past and the whole house would smell like onion, and whoever cut it would start crying within seconds. Cut most onions today and you can chop a whole handful and barely notice a smell at all.

Same with garlic: it can take eight or ten cloves now to get the flavor one clove used to carry.

When did you last cry cutting an onion?
